title: Meaning Feudalism at the Guidance Layer: Sovereign Enclosure of the Composition Layer in Google's June 2026 SEO/AEO/GEO Canonicalization (v1.2)
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
This v1.2 critique reads a June 2026 revision to Google Search Central’s “Do you need an SEO?” guidance as jurisdictional consolidation. It identifies four moves: naming AEO/GEO without defining the practice; warning that third-party tools lack internal ranking data; directing complaints about deceptive providers toward the Federal Trade Commission; and recommending Google Search Console as the canonical first-party instrument.

The work calls these taxonomic capture, telemetry starvation, conscription of state enforcement, and an oath of fealty. Its argument is that platform guidance can become more than product documentation by defining professional categories, accepted measurement, complaint routes, and the preferred ledger through which a population understands performance. It distinguishes composition-layer measurement from ordinary ranking analytics and argues that public accountability requires external observation precisely because investigators lack internal data.

The body’s revised wording describes state enforcement as a structural risk rather than a completed fact: FTC discretion remains independent, and the paper does not show that the agency adopted Google guidance as law. The feudal and sovereignty language remains interpretive. Google’s accurate statement that third parties lack internal data does not itself invalidate external tools; whether guidance materially reduces independent measurement is empirical.

A durable evidence package should preserve the exact page revision, prior version, timestamps, diffs, reports, and later changes.

wiki_article:
**Meaning Feudalism at the Guidance Layer** is a 2026 critique by Lee Sharks of changes to Google’s public SEO guidance.

It identifies official naming of AEO/GEO, warnings about third-party measurement, referral of deceptive-business complaints to the FTC, and recommendation of Google Search Console.

It interprets these as a jurisdictional structure in which one platform helps define the profession, accepted measurement, complaint route, and preferred tool.

The analysis does not establish that the FTC treats Google guidance as law or that independent tools are invalid.
